Things that come from trees.Maple syrup: Maple syrup is boiled from tree sap, taking about 40 litres to make one litre. Sap runs best when nights freeze and days warm.
Things that come from trees.Cork: Cork is the bark of the cork oak, harvested by hand every nine years or so. The tree is not killed and grows new bark.
Things that come from trees.Natural rubber: Natural rubber is latex tapped from the rubber tree, originally from the Amazon. Collectors cut a thin groove in the bark and the milk runs out into a cup.
Things that come from trees.Paper: Paper is made mostly from tree wood pulp. Papermakers also use recycled fibre, and a tree can yield thousands of sheets.
Things that come from trees.Cinnamon: Cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree, peeled and rolled into quills as it dries. Ceylon cinnamon is the paler and milder kind.
Things that come from trees.Cocoa: Cocoa comes from beans in pods growing directly on the trunk of the cacao tree. It takes about 400 beans to make one kilo of chocolate.
Things that come from trees.Olive oil: Olive oil is pressed from the fruit of olive trees, which can live for well over 1,000 years. Some trees in the Mediterranean are said to be older.
Things that come from trees.Amber: Amber is fossilised tree resin millions of years old. Sometimes it holds insects, and even small lizards, preserved in perfect detail.
Things that come from trees.Coconut: Coconut is the fruit of the coconut palm, which is a tree-like plant. It can float across oceans, and spread across tropical shores that way.
Things that come from trees.Turpentine: Turpentine is distilled from pine resin. It was once a key ingredient in paint thinners and varnish.
Things that come from trees.Nutmeg: Nutmeg comes from the seed of a tree, and mace from its covering. Nutmeg was once so precious that the Dutch swapped Manhattan for a nutmeg island.
Things that come from trees.Walnut: Walnuts grow on walnut trees. Their shells are used in cleaning products, and the wood is prized for furniture and gunstocks.
Things that come from trees.Silk: Silk comes from silkworm cocoons, not trees. Worms eat mulberry leaves, but the thread is made by the insect.
Things that come from trees.Wool: Wool is the fleece of sheep and other animals. It stays warm even when damp because the fibres absorb moisture.
Things that come from trees.Cotton: Cotton grows on a shrubby plant as fluffy bolls. It's the most important natural fibre, and its seeds hold oil, too.
Things that come from trees.Linen: Linen is woven from the stems of the flax plant. It's among the oldest textiles, used in ancient Egyptian mummy wrappings.
Things that come from trees.Honey: Honey is made by bees from flower nectar. It's a sticky product of an insect, not a tree, though bees often nest in tree hollows.
Things that come from trees.Leather: Leather is tanned animal hide. The tanning process turns it from perishable skin into a stable material, a craft thousands of years old.
Things that come from trees.Pearl: Pearls are made by molluscs like oysters. They are one of the few gems made by a living animal.
Things that come from trees.Vanilla: Vanilla comes from the pod of an orchid vine. It's the second most expensive spice, after saffron, because the flowers must be hand-pollinated.
Things that come from trees.Cane sugar: Cane sugar comes from the stalks of sugarcane, a giant grass. Not a tree product, though sugar maples make a different sugar.
Things that come from trees.Saffron: Saffron is the thread-like stigma of a crocus flower. It takes about 150,000 flowers to produce a kilo, making it the priciest spice.
Things that come from trees.Ivory: Ivory comes from the tusks of elephants and similar animals, which are teeth. The international trade in it is banned.
Things that come from trees.Peanut: The peanut is a legume that grows underground, so it's not a tree nut. The plant flowers above ground and then pushes the pod into the soil.

Countries bordering Russia.Norway: Russia and Norway share a short Arctic border near Kirkenes, one of the few where NATO meets Russia directly.
Countries bordering Russia.Finland: At about 1,300 km, this is Russia's longest border with an EU country, and it has been largely closed since 2023.
Countries bordering Russia.Estonia: Estonia's border runs along Lake Peipus and through the town of Narva, which faces Russian Ivangorod across a river.
Countries bordering Russia.Latvia: Latvia's eastern border with Russia is short, and the country has a large Russian-speaking minority.
Countries bordering Russia.Lithuania: Lithuania borders Russia only through the exclave of Kaliningrad, a Russian region cut off from the mainland.
Countries bordering Russia.Poland: Poland touches Russia only through the Kaliningrad exclave, a small piece of Russia on the Baltic.
Countries bordering Russia.Belarus: Belarus is Russia's close ally, and the two have an open border and a so-called Union State.
Countries bordering Russia.Ukraine: Ukraine has one of Russia's longest borders, over 1,900 km, stretching from Belarus to the Sea of Azov.
Countries bordering Russia.Georgia: Georgia borders Russia in the Caucasus, where the Greater Caucasus mountains form a natural wall.
Countries bordering Russia.Azerbaijan: Azerbaijan meets Russia at the Caucasus, on the Caspian side, close to Russia's Dagestan.
Countries bordering Russia.Kazakhstan: The Russia-Kazakhstan border is the longest continuous land border in the world, at over 7,500 km.
Countries bordering Russia.China: The border with China is more than 4,000 km long and was settled in 2004.
Countries bordering Russia.Mongolia: Mongolia borders Russia and China only, and is landlocked between the two.
Countries bordering Russia.North Korea: Russia and North Korea share a tiny border, only about 17 km, along the Tumen River.
Countries bordering Russia.Sweden: Sweden and Russia face each other across the Baltic, but have no land border, a common slip because Finland lies between.
Countries bordering Russia.Hungary: Hungary and Russia are separated by Ukraine and Slovakia, so they have no shared border.
Countries bordering Russia.Turkey: Turkey and Russia are neighbors across the Black Sea, but Georgia and the sea lie between them on land.
Countries bordering Russia.Armenia: Armenia is in the Caucasus but its neighbors are Georgia, Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran, not Russia.
Countries bordering Russia.Moldova: Moldova is wedged between Romania and Ukraine, so it doesn't touch Russia, though Russian troops are in Transnistria.
Countries bordering Russia.Romania: Romania borders Ukraine and Moldova to the east, and not Russia, though it lies on the Black Sea coast too.
Countries bordering Russia.Iran: Iran and Russia face each other across the Caspian Sea, so there's no land border between them.
Countries bordering Russia.Germany: Germany lies far to the west, with Poland and the Baltic Sea between it and Russia.
Countries bordering Russia.Uzbekistan: Uzbekistan is doubly landlocked, and Kazakhstan lies between it and Russia, so they never touch.
Countries bordering Russia.South Korea: South Korea and Russia are neighbors only across the sea, since North Korea sits in between on land.

Cities on the Rhine.Basel: This Swiss city is where the Rhine turns north, and the river forms a border with France and Germany. It has its own annual carnival, Fasnacht.
Cities on the Rhine.Strasbourg: The French city sits right on the Rhine and hosts the European Parliament. Its cathedral was the tallest building on Earth until the 19th century.
Cities on the Rhine.Mainz: Germany's city at the junction of Rhine and Main, where Gutenberg printed his famous Bible in the 1450s. It claims to be the birthplace of modern printing.
Cities on the Rhine.Cologne: Its giant Gothic cathedral on the Rhine took over 600 years to complete. Eau de Cologne, a perfume, was created here in 1709.
Cities on the Rhine.Düsseldorf: The Rhine city is known for its old-town bars, where altbier is brewed, and it has a long tradition of fashion and Japanese expats.
Cities on the Rhine.Bonn: This Rhine city was the capital of West Germany until 1990, and it's Beethoven's birthplace, in 1770.
Cities on the Rhine.Koblenz: At the Deutsches Eck, the Moselle flows into the Rhine. The city name comes from Latin for confluence.
Cities on the Rhine.Mannheim: Its city center is laid out on a grid, and it sits at the Rhine and Neckar confluence. Its streets are labeled with letters and numbers instead of names.
Cities on the Rhine.Duisburg: Its inland port is the world's largest, where the Ruhr meets the Rhine. Steel and coal once built the city.
Cities on the Rhine.Schaffhausen: A Swiss town on the Rhine near the Rhine Falls, Europe's largest plain waterfall, which drops about 23 m.
Cities on the Rhine.Arnhem: This Dutch city is on the Nederrijn, a branch of the Rhine. The World War II battle of Arnhem was about taking its bridge.
Cities on the Rhine.Frankfurt: Frankfurt is on the Main, a tributary of the Rhine. It's close to the Rhine, but not on it.
Cities on the Rhine.Munich: It stands on the Isar, which flows to the Danube. Munich is nowhere near the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Stuttgart: Stuttgart lies on the Neckar, which flows into the Rhine at Mannheim, not directly on the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Hamburg: Germany's big port sits on the Elbe, flowing to the North Sea, and not on the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Berlin: The capital stands on the Spree, a tributary of the Havel and Elbe, far from the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Paris: France's capital sits on the Seine. The Rhine lies on its eastern border.
Cities on the Rhine.Lyon: Lyon is on the Rhône and the Saône, not on the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Zurich: Zurich sits on a lake and the Limmat, which flows to the Aare and then to the Rhine. It isn't on the Rhine itself.
Cities on the Rhine.Vienna: Austria's capital lies on the Danube, not on the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Hanover: It sits on the Leine, a tributary of the Weser, flowing north to the North Sea, far from the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Brussels: Belgium's capital is on the little river Senne, which is a tributary of the Scheldt, not the Rhine.
Cities on the Rhine.Luxembourg: The city sits on the Alzette, a tributary of the Sauer and Moselle, which joins the Rhine at Koblenz, so it's near but not on it.
Cities on the Rhine.Geneva: It sits on Lake Geneva where the Rhône leaves it. The Rhône flows to the Mediterranean, so the Rhine is not involved.

Landmarks in Greece.Acropolis: The citadel above Athens has stood for nearly 2,500 years, and was a place of worship long before the Parthenon was built.
Landmarks in Greece.Parthenon: The temple of Athena was built in the 5th century BC, and its sculptures, the Elgin Marbles, are claimed by Greece from the British Museum.
Landmarks in Greece.Delphi: Ancient Greeks considered Delphi the centre of the world, where the Pythia oracle delivered prophecies, sometimes thought to be inspired by gases.
Landmarks in Greece.Meteora: Monasteries perched on towering sandstone pillars, reached once only by ladders and nets hauled up by rope.
Landmarks in Greece.Mount Olympus: Greece's highest peak, at about 2,917 metres, was the mythical home of the twelve gods, and was first climbed in 1913.
Landmarks in Greece.Knossos: The Minoan palace on Crete, linked to the legend of the Minotaur and the labyrinth, was unearthed by Arthur Evans in 1900.
Landmarks in Greece.Santorini: The island's caldera comes from a huge volcanic eruption about 3,600 years ago, which some link to the Atlantis legend.
Landmarks in Greece.Olympia: The birthplace of the ancient Olympic Games, held here every four years from 776 BC, and where the modern torch is lit.
Landmarks in Greece.Mykonos: A Cycladic island with whitewashed windmills and a famous party scene, it has a pelican named Petros as its mascot.
Landmarks in Greece.Corfu: This Ionian island has Venetian, French and British influences, and is where Prince Philip was born.
Landmarks in Greece.Thessaloniki: Greece's second city, named for Alexander the Great's half-sister, and has a famous White Tower on the waterfront.
Landmarks in Greece.Epidaurus: Its ancient theatre seats about 14,000 and is so acoustically perfect that a whisper on stage can reach the top row.
Landmarks in Greece.Ephesus: The ancient Greek city in Turkey held the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders, and a great library.
Landmarks in Greece.Troy: The legendary city of the Trojan War has ruins in northwest Turkey, excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in the 1870s.
Landmarks in Greece.Hagia Sophia: Istanbul's great domed building was a church for about 900 years, then a mosque, a museum, and a mosque again.
Landmarks in Greece.Pamukkale: Turkish terraces of white travertine pools, whose name means cotton castle, with ancient Hierapolis spa ruins on top.
Landmarks in Greece.Cappadocia: A Turkish region of fairy chimneys and cave dwellings, famous for sunrise hot-air balloons.
Landmarks in Greece.Colosseum: Rome's amphitheatre could seat about 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights and was finished around 80 AD, so it's in Italy.
Landmarks in Greece.Pompeii: A Roman city in Italy buried by Vesuvius in 79 AD, preserved in ash, including bakery loaves and graffiti.
Landmarks in Greece.Carthage: Rome's great rival was a Phoenician city in what is now Tunisia, which Rome destroyed in 146 BC.
Landmarks in Greece.Valletta: The capital of Malta, built by the Knights of St John, is one of Europe's smallest capitals.
Landmarks in Greece.Dubrovnik: A walled Croatian city on the Adriatic, called the Pearl of the Adriatic, which served as King's Landing in Game of Thrones.
Landmarks in Greece.Cyprus: The Mediterranean island is its own country, with a long Greek-speaking history, but isn't part of mainland Greece.
Landmarks in Greece.Bodrum: A Turkish resort on the Aegean, site of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, a wonder of the ancient world.

Things that dissolve in water.Salt: Water molecules pull sodium and chloride ions apart, which is why salt vanishes. The ocean holds enough dissolved salt to cover the land in a deep layer.
Things that dissolve in water.Sugar: Sugar dissolves far better in hot water than cold, which is how rock candy grows: crystals form as a hot syrup cools.
Things that dissolve in water.Baking soda: Baking soda dissolves in water, and it can fizz with acids. Dissolved, it makes the solution slightly alkaline.
Things that dissolve in water.Instant coffee: Instant coffee is brewed coffee dried into soluble crystals, a process that took off after wartime rations.
Things that dissolve in water.Citric acid: Found in lemons and limes, citric acid dissolves readily in water. It's also added to sour candy and used in cleaners.
Things that dissolve in water.Epsom salt: Despite the name it isn't table salt, it's magnesium sulfate. Named for a bath spring town in Surrey, England.
Things that dissolve in water.Honey: Honey dissolves in water but is thick enough to sink in a blob first. Honey is sugary enough that it never really spoils.
Things that dissolve in water.Ethanol: Ethanol mixes with water in every proportion, which is why distilled spirits can be diluted to any strength.
Things that dissolve in water.Vinegar: Vinegar is mostly water with about 5 percent acetic acid, so it blends fully. The name means 'sour wine' in French.
Things that dissolve in water.Food coloring: Food coloring is made of water-soluble dyes. A drop spreads through a glass on its own, because molecules constantly jostle and mix.
Things that dissolve in water.Carbon dioxide: CO2 does dissolve in water, forming a weak acid called carbonic acid. That dissolved gas is what gives soda fizz, and it acidifies the oceans.
Things that dissolve in water.Ammonia: Ammonia is extremely soluble, and a household cleaner is just ammonia gas dissolved in water.
Things that dissolve in water.Olive oil: Oil is nonpolar, so water molecules won't mix with it. It floats on top because it's less dense than water.
Things that dissolve in water.Sand: Sand is mostly quartz, which water barely dissolves at all. Over millions of years, though, it does erode, but not in a cup.
Things that dissolve in water.Candle wax: Wax is a nonpolar hydrocarbon and repels water, which is why it's used for waterproofing. It floats too.
Things that dissolve in water.Chalk: Chalk is calcium carbonate, which barely dissolves in pure water. Acid rain can slowly eat away at it, though.
Things that dissolve in water.Flour: Flour stirs into water as a cloudy suspension, not a solution. Starch grains stay solid and eventually settle.
Things that dissolve in water.Butter: Butter is fat with some water, so it melts rather than dissolves. It separates into floating fat when mixed with water.
Things that dissolve in water.Black pepper: Pepper stays as specks because its flavor compound, piperine, is not water-soluble. It dissolves in oil or alcohol instead.
Things that dissolve in water.Plastic: Most plastic doesn't dissolve in water, which is why it piles up in oceans. Some special plastics like PVA do dissolve.
Things that dissolve in water.Gold: Gold is notoriously unreactive and won't dissolve in water, or in any single acid. Only aqua regia, a mix of two acids, dissolves it.
Things that dissolve in water.Rubber: Rubber just sits there in water, waterproof by nature. That's why raincoats and boots are made from it.
Things that dissolve in water.Glitter: Glitter is tiny bits of plastic and metallic film that don't dissolve, which is why it's so hard to wash out and counts as microplastic.
Things that dissolve in water.Pebbles: Pebbles are rock, and water barely dissolves them in any short span. Rivers wear them smooth by tumbling, not by dissolving.

Villains from kids' cartoons.Skeletor: He-Man's skull-faced enemy rules from Snake Mountain. In Masters of the Universe lore he is Keldor, He-Man's own uncle, who turned to evil.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Dr. Claw: The unseen villain of Inspector Gadget, shown only as a gloved hand stroking a cat named MAD Cat. His face is never revealed.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Mumm-Ra: The ancient sorcerer priest of ThunderCats, who transforms from a mummy to a powerful form to fight Lion-O.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Shredder: Oroku Saki leads the Foot Clan against the Turtles. In the original 1984 comic he died in the very first issue.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Mojo Jojo: The chimp who is the archenemy of The Powerpuff Girls. He gained super intelligence in an accident and speaks in long monologues.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Plankton: The tiny green schemer who wants the Krabby Patty secret formula. Plankton is a copepod, a real tiny crustacean found in oceans.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Dr. Doofenshmirtz: The scientist in Phineas and Ferb whose evil schemes involve an inator device. He is from the fictional village of Gimmelshtump.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Gargamel: The wizard who hunts Smurfs, with his cat Azrael. He appears in Peyo's Belgian comics from 1958, before the TV show.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Swiper: The sneaky fox in Dora the Explorer who snatches things, and can only be stopped by saying Swiper, no swiping three times.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Cobra Commander: The hooded leader of Cobra, the terrorist organization fighting G.I. Joe in the 1980s toy line and cartoon. His fans debate his face.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Megatron: The Decepticon leader transformed into a handgun in the original 1980s toy line. His rival is Optimus Prime.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Dick Dastardly: Whose cheating always backfires in Wacky Races, often to the snicker of his dog Muttley. He has never once won.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Aku: The shape-shifting demon of Samurai Jack who flings the samurai into a dystopian future. Genndy Tartakovsky created the series.
Villains from kids' cartoons.He-Man: The hero of Masters of the Universe, who holds up a sword and shouts I have the power. A good guy, so no.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Inspector Gadget: A bumbling cyborg detective, a hero. His niece Penny and dog Brain solve the cases while he takes the credit.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Lion-O: The hero of ThunderCats, a cat-like warrior who leads against Mumm-Ra and wields the Sword of Omens.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Leonardo: The Turtles' leader is named after Leonardo da Vinci, and wears a blue mask. He is a hero, not a villain.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Blossom: The leader of The Powerpuff Girls, the pink one. A hero made from sugar, spice and Chemical X.
Villains from kids' cartoons.SpongeBob: The sponge is a fry cook at the Krabby Patty. He is the hero Plankton wants to defeat.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Perry the Platypus: Perry is Agent P, a secret agent platypus who only chatters. He foils Doofenshmirtz and is a hero.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Papa Smurf: The Smurfs' leader, who is hundreds of years old according to lore. He wears a red hat and keeps Gargamel at bay.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Dora: The explorer who asks viewers for help. She is the heroine, not the villain, and her nemesis is Swiper.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Optimus Prime: Leader of the heroic Autobots, who transforms into a truck. Peter Cullen has voiced him since the 1980s.
Villains from kids' cartoons.Penny: Penny is Inspector Gadget's clever niece who solves the cases. She's a hero, not a villain.

Tuned (pitched) percussion.Xylophone: Wooden bars struck by mallets give a bright, short note, and each bar is tuned to a fixed pitch.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Marimba: The marimba is deeper and warmer than a xylophone, thanks to resonator tubes under each wooden bar.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Glockenspiel: The name is German for 'bell play', and its metal bars ring like small bells.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Vibraphone: Motor-driven fans in the resonators give the vibraphone its trademark vibrato.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Timpani: Timpani are the trap here: unlike most drums, pedals tune them to specific notes.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Tubular bells: Orchestral tubular bells imitate church bells, and each tube gives a precise pitched note.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Steel drum: Steel drums from Trinidad began as oil barrels hammered into tuned notes.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Kalimba: The kalimba is a thumb piano whose metal tines each play a pitch, related to the African mbira.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Handbells: Each handbell plays a single note, so ringers combine to play tunes.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Snare drum: The snare drum has no definite pitch, so it counts as unpitched percussion.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Bass drum: The bass drum gives a deep thud but no exact note, so it's not a melodic instrument.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Cymbal: Cymbals crash with an indefinite pitch, a wash of overtones rather than one tuned note.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Triangle: A triangle's ring is bright but not tied to a particular note, so it's unpitched.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Maracas: Maracas are shakers whose seeds rattle with no specific pitch.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Tambourine: A tambourine jingles with metal discs, and while some are tuned, most have no fixed pitch.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Castanets: Castanets click without a pitch, and give rhythm in flamenco.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Cowbell: A cowbell has a pitch of sorts but isn't part of a tuned set, so it counts as unpitched.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Woodblock: A woodblock gives a dry knock with no precise pitch, even though blocks come in sizes.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Claves: Claves are two sticks clacked together, giving a bright click with no fixed note.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Guiro: A guiro is a ridged gourd scraped for a rasp, with no pitch.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Shaker: Shakers make a rustling noise rather than a note, and they come in many forms around the world.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Hi-hat: A hi-hat is a pair of cymbals closed with a pedal, so unpitched and used for rhythm.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Washboard: A washboard is a ridged scraper for rhythm in folk and zydeco, and gives no tuned notes.
Tuned (pitched) percussion.Rainstick: A rainstick makes a cascade of rustle, not a note.

Bands with a female lead singer.Blondie: Debbie Harry fronted the New York band, which hit number one with Heart of Glass in 1979. Blondie was her nickname from street catcalls.
Bands with a female lead singer.No Doubt: Gwen Stefani led the Anaheim ska-punk band, whose 1995 album Tragic Kingdom sold over 10 million copies in the US.
Bands with a female lead singer.Paramore: Hayley Williams joined the band at age 13 in Franklin, Tennessee. Their song Misery Business remains a signature hit.
Bands with a female lead singer.The Cranberries: Dolores O'Riordan, from Limerick, Ireland, led them. Her yodel-like vocals shaped Zombie, a 1994 protest song about the Troubles.
Bands with a female lead singer.Evanescence: Amy Lee's piano and soaring voice drove Bring Me to Life, from their 2003 debut Fallen, which sold millions.
Bands with a female lead singer.Garbage: Scottish singer Shirley Manson fronted this band, formed in Wisconsin by producers including Butch Vig, who also produced Nirvana's Nevermind.
Bands with a female lead singer.Heart: Sisters Ann and Nancy Wilson led them. Ann's powerful voice helped make them hard rock pioneers, with hits like Barracuda.
Bands with a female lead singer.The Pretenders: Chrissie Hynde, an Ohio native, formed the band in London in 1978. She remains its only constant member.
Bands with a female lead singer.Eurythmics: Annie Lennox and Dave Stewart's 1983 hit Sweet Dreams has a distinctive synth riff. Lennox's androgynous look was part of their image.
Bands with a female lead singer.The Bangles: The all-female California group had a 1986 hit with Walk Like an Egyptian. Prince wrote their hit Manic Monday.
Bands with a female lead singer.Yeah Yeah Yeahs: Karen O leads the New York art-rock trio. Their 2006 song Maps is often named among the best love songs of its decade.
Bands with a female lead singer.Hole: Courtney Love fronted the band, whose 1994 album Live Through This came out days after Kurt Cobain's death.
Bands with a female lead singer.Coldplay: Chris Martin sings lead. Their 2000 debut Parachutes includes Yellow, and the band formed in London at university.
Bands with a female lead singer.Oasis: Liam Gallagher sang while brother Noel wrote the songs. Their rivalry with Blur helped define Britpop in the mid-1990s.
Bands with a female lead singer.U2: Bono has fronted the Dublin band since the 1970s. The band formed when the members were teenagers answering a notice on a school board.
Bands with a female lead singer.Green Day: Billie Joe Armstrong has sung with them since the band formed in Berkeley in 1987. American Idiot, from 2004, became a stage musical.
Bands with a female lead singer.The Killers: Brandon Flowers leads the Las Vegas band. Their debut album Hot Fuss has Mr. Brightside, a UK chart staple for years.
Bands with a female lead singer.Maroon 5: Adam Levine has been the main voice, and the group began as Kara's Flowers in high school. Their hit Moves Like Jagger featured Christina Aguilera.
Bands with a female lead singer.Linkin Park: Chester Bennington shared vocals with Mike Shinoda. Their 2000 debut Hybrid Theory is one of the best-selling debut albums of the century.
Bands with a female lead singer.Nirvana: Kurt Cobain was the singer. Nevermind in 1991 pushed grunge into the mainstream and knocked Michael Jackson off number one.
Bands with a female lead singer.Radiohead: Thom Yorke is the lead singer. They've been praised for OK Computer in 1997, and they released In Rainbows as pay-what-you-want.
Bands with a female lead singer.Pearl Jam: Eddie Vedder joined the Seattle band after getting a demo tape in the mail from San Diego. The band later fought Ticketmaster.
Bands with a female lead singer.The Police: Sting sang and played bass. The trio's name suits its hit Every Breath You Take, often misread as a love song, but it's about surveillance.
Bands with a female lead singer.Metallica: James Hetfield has sung the heavy metal band's songs since 1981. Their 1991 self-titled Black Album was a huge seller.

Nirvana songs.Come as You Are: Its jangly riff echoes Killing Joke's Eighties, and Kurt Cobain's watery guitar tone came from a chorus pedal.
Nirvana songs.Lithium: On Nevermind, its narrator seeks comfort in religion after a loss; the mood swings between calm verses and screaming choruses, like the title drug.
Nirvana songs.Heart-Shaped Box: From In Utero, 1993; the video by Anton Corbijn is full of strange religious and medical imagery.
Nirvana songs.In Bloom: It pokes fun at fans who sing along without understanding the lyrics, which makes it ironic that it became a sing-along.
Nirvana songs.All Apologies: A closing track on In Utero, 1993, and a highlight of Nirvana's MTV Unplugged set, which was recorded months before Cobain died.
Nirvana songs.About a Girl: A Bleach-era pop song about Cobain's girlfriend, with a Beatles-like melody; the Unplugged version brought it fame.
Nirvana songs.Polly: Sung from the viewpoint of a kidnapper, based on a real 1987 abduction in Washington state; the acoustic Nevermind song is unsettling on purpose.
Nirvana songs.Dumb: From In Utero; a plain, wry song about trying to be content, with a cello adding a gentle, sad edge.
Nirvana songs.Breed: Originally titled Imodium, a joke name that the band later dropped; it's a fast Nevermind riff-fest.
Nirvana songs.Black Hole Sun: Soundgarden, 1994. Chris Cornell's surreal song was Seattle's other big grunge hit, but not Nirvana's.
Nirvana songs.Jeremy: Pearl Jam, inspired by a real teenager's suicide in a Texas school; Nirvana's Seattle peers, not Nirvana.
Nirvana songs.Even Flow: A Pearl Jam track from Ten, from the same Seattle scene and the same era, but another band.
Nirvana songs.Plush: Stone Temple Pilots, 1992. Critics said STP copied Seattle grunge, though they came from San Diego.
Nirvana songs.Man in the Box: Alice in Chains, 1990; Layne Staley's dark harmonies are classic Seattle grunge, but another band.
Nirvana songs.Interstate Love Song: Stone Temple Pilots' 1994 ballad, a slow-burning radio hit; not Nirvana.
Nirvana songs.Creep: Radiohead's 1992 debut, whose crunchy guitar bursts were Jonny Greenwood's attempt to ruin the song.
Nirvana songs.Alive: Pearl Jam's 1991 song, with a clean, bright riff; a Seattle contemporary, not Nirvana.
Nirvana songs.Zombie: The Cranberries wrote it about two children killed in the 1993 Warrington bombing; Irish, not Nirvana.
Nirvana songs.Basket Case: Green Day, 1994. Billie Joe Armstrong wrote it about his panic attacks, in a punk style unlike Nirvana's.
Nirvana songs.Everlong: A trap: Foo Fighters, 1997, formed by Dave Grohl, Nirvana's former drummer, but it's his own band's song.
Nirvana songs.Wonderwall: Oasis, 1995. Noel Gallagher's best-known song is Britpop, not grunge.
Nirvana songs.Song 2: Blur, 1997. Its Woo-hoo chorus began as a joke parody of grunge, which is why it feels like Nirvana but isn't.
Nirvana songs.Losing My Religion: R.E.M., 1991. The title is Southern slang for reaching the end of your rope, with no religious meaning.
Nirvana songs.Under the Bridge: Red Hot Chili Peppers, 1991; Anthony Kiedis wrote it about loneliness in Los Angeles, in a funk-rock style that is far from Nirvana.

Ed Sheeran songs.Shape of You: A worldwide hit in 2017, and Sheeran later added the writers of TLC's No Scrubs as co-writers because the melody was similar.
Ed Sheeran songs.Perfect: A wedding favorite from 2017, written for his future wife, Cherry Seaborn; it was the UK Christmas number one that year.
Ed Sheeran songs.Thinking Out Loud: It won the Grammy for Song of the Year in 2016; Sheeran later won a court case claiming he copied Marvin Gaye's Let's Get It On.
Ed Sheeran songs.Photograph: Co-written with Johnny McDaid of Snow Patrol; its video is a montage of Sheeran's childhood home movies.
Ed Sheeran songs.The A Team: His 2011 debut hit about a prostitute struggling with drugs was inspired by a visit to a homeless shelter.
Ed Sheeran songs.Castle on the Hill: A look back at his hometown, Framlingham in Suffolk, with a fiddle and a pop beat.
Ed Sheeran songs.Galway Girl: An Irish folk-pop song with the band Beoga, and Steve Earle had another song of the same name long before.
Ed Sheeran songs.Bad Habits: Sheeran's 2021 comeback single hit UK number one and topped charts across Europe, with a synth-driven dance-pop beat.
Ed Sheeran songs.Shivers: A 2021 number one in the UK, written with a catchy, dance-leaning chorus that took over radio that autumn.
Ed Sheeran songs.Sing: A 2014 song produced by Pharrell Williams, with a funky groove that surprised his folk fans.
Ed Sheeran songs.Lego House: Rupert Grint, who played Ron in Harry Potter, stars in the music video, as a boyfriend caught in a heartbreak.
Ed Sheeran songs.Eyes Closed: A 2023 song written in the wake of friend Jamal Edwards's death.
Ed Sheeran songs.Someone You Loved: Lewis Capaldi, 2018, a Scottish singer-songwriter's hit; not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Let Her Go: Passenger, 2012, a busker-style folk song by Mike Rosenberg; not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Stay with Me: Sam Smith, 2014. Tom Petty received a writing credit after it resembled I Won't Back Down.
Ed Sheeran songs.All of Me: John Legend, 2013; a piano ballad written for Chrissy Teigen, his future wife, not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Hold Back the River: James Bay, 2014; a folk-rock hit with a stomp-and-clap chorus, not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Budapest: George Ezra, 2014; the Hertfordshire singer's baritone hit is a song about a travel dream.
Ed Sheeran songs.Shotgun: George Ezra, 2018, another travel-themed song; not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Riptide: Vance Joy, 2013; the Australian's hit uses a ukulele and was popular on TikTok.
Ed Sheeran songs.Ho Hey: The Lumineers, 2012, a Denver folk band that made stomping singalongs; not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Before You Go: Lewis Capaldi, 2019, from his debut album; not Sheeran.
Ed Sheeran songs.Counting Stars: OneRepublic, 2013, a pop-rock band's hit that sits close to Sheeran's folk-pop but isn't his.
Ed Sheeran songs.Grenade: Bruno Mars, 2010, a bitter breakup song; not Sheeran.

Chess terms.Checkmate: Checkmate comes from the Persian shah mat, often translated as the king is helpless, and a game ends the moment it happens.
Chess terms.Castling: Castling is the only move that shifts two pieces at once, and you cannot do it if the king is in check or has moved.
Chess terms.En passant: En passant is a special pawn capture that exists because a pawn's two-square first move was introduced and would otherwise let it dodge capture.
Chess terms.Stalemate: Stalemate is a draw, not a win: when a player has no legal move but isn't in check, the game ends level.
Chess terms.Gambit: A gambit sacrifices a pawn or piece early for position, and the Queen's Gambit gave its name to a hit 2020 series.
Chess terms.Fork: A fork is a move that attacks two pieces at once, and knights are especially good at it because of their jumping route.
Chess terms.Pin: A pin freezes a piece because moving it would expose a more valuable one behind it, and an absolute pin involves the king.
Chess terms.Skewer: A skewer is a reverse pin: the more valuable piece must move, which exposes the lesser piece behind it to capture.
Chess terms.Fianchetto: Fianchetto comes from the Italian for little flank, and it means developing a bishop to b2 or g2 where it eyes the long diagonal.
Chess terms.Zugzwang: Zugzwang is German for compulsion to move: it means any move a player makes will worsen their position, a state the rest of life rarely allows.
Chess terms.Rook: The rook was once a chariot, which explains the move in straight lines, and it is worth about five pawns.
Chess terms.Bishop: Bishops are worth about three pawns, and each stays on one color of square for the whole game, so there is a light-squared and dark-squared bishop.
Chess terms.Bluff: Bluff belongs to poker, not chess: since chess has no hidden information, nothing can be hidden from the opponent.
Chess terms.Trump: A trump is a card game term, where a suit outranks others, and chess has no way to make one piece outrank all.
Chess terms.Flush: A flush in poker is about a one-in-500 hand; chess has no hands and no hidden cards, so nothing like it exists here.
Chess terms.Birdie: Birdie is a golf score of one under par, and it gets its name from early 1900s slang for something excellent.
Chess terms.Deuce: Deuce probably comes from the French à deux, meaning two points are needed to win: a tennis standoff, not a chess one.
Chess terms.Strike: A strike belongs to bowling and baseball, and in chess you can't strike anything in the same way.
Chess terms.Bullseye: A bullseye in darts is worth 50 points, and the outer bull is 25, but there is no target on a chessboard.
Chess terms.Yahtzee: Edwin Lowe bought this dice game from a Canadian couple who played it on their yacht, hence the name, and sold millions.
Chess terms.Uno: Uno is a card game created in 1971 by an Ohio barber named Merle Robbins, who sold it from his barbershop.
Chess terms.Touchdown: The name comes from rugby, where the ball had to be touched down; American football kept it though the ball need not touch the ground.
Chess terms.Hat trick: A hat trick is three goals in one game, usually soccer or hockey, and the name began in cricket for three wickets in a row.
Chess terms.Slam dunk: College basketball banned the dunk from 1967 to 1976, widely seen as aimed at Lew Alcindor, and it has no place in chess.

Tenpin bowling terms.Strike: A strike knocks down all ten pins with the first ball, and three in a row is a turkey.
Tenpin bowling terms.Spare: A spare clears all pins in two balls, and it scores ten plus the next roll as a bonus.
Tenpin bowling terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball falls in the channel and scores nothing; bumpers are often put up so children cannot throw one.
Tenpin bowling terms.Split: A split leaves pins standing with a gap between them, and the 7-10 split is notoriously difficult to convert.
Tenpin bowling terms.Turkey: Three strikes in a row make a turkey, and four are sometimes called a hambone, a bowling-alley nickname that stuck.
Tenpin bowling terms.Lane: A lane is 60 feet from foul line to head pin and 41.5 inches wide, and is coated in patterns of oil that change how the ball behaves.
Tenpin bowling terms.Frame: A game has ten frames, and in the tenth a bowler who strikes or spares earns extra rolls.
Tenpin bowling terms.Foul line: The foul line marks the start of the lane, and stepping over it scores a zero for that delivery.
Tenpin bowling terms.Perfect game: A perfect game is 300, made of twelve straight strikes, and is called a perfect game since there is no higher score.
Tenpin bowling terms.Hook: A hook is a curving throw achieved by rotating the ball, and it improves the angle into the pins.
Tenpin bowling terms.Pins: Pins are 15 inches tall and weigh about 3 pounds, and a ten-pin setup forms a triangle.
Tenpin bowling terms.Birdie: A birdie is golf's one under par, and in bowling a score under par isn't a thing.
Tenpin bowling terms.Love: Love is tennis's zero, and bowling's zero is a miss or a gutter ball.
Tenpin bowling terms.Wicket: Wicket is cricket's; the cricket bowler aims at stumps, much as a tenpin bowler aims at the pins, but one sends a hard ball bouncing.
Tenpin bowling terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is football's, and in bowling the thrill is a strike.
Tenpin bowling terms.Puck: A puck is hockey's, and a bowling ball is drilled with finger holes and weighs up to 16 pounds.
Tenpin bowling terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball's, and bowling's big moment is a perfect game.
Tenpin bowling terms.Bunt: A bunt is baseball's, though in bowling a lightly rolled ball is a mere pick-up.
Tenpin bowling terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess; bowling's thinking is lane play, where oil patterns change.
Tenpin bowling terms.Try: A try is rugby's, worth five points, and in bowling you get two tries a frame.
Tenpin bowling terms.Header: A header is soccer's head-ball; in bowling the head pin is the front one, the 1-pin, and hitting it slightly off-center is the aim.
Tenpin bowling terms.Ace: An ace is tennis's unreturned serve, and bowling's near cousin is a strike.
Tenpin bowling terms.Deuce: A deuce is tennis's 40-all; in bowling slang it's a two-count for a frame.
Tenpin bowling terms.Bullseye: A bullseye is darts and archery's center, and bowling's best target is the pocket between the head pin and the next.

Card games.Poker: A royal flush appears about once in 650,000 five-card hands, so most players go a lifetime without seeing one.
Card games.Blackjack: Blackjack's card counting was popularized by mathematician Edward Thorp's 1962 book Beat the Dealer, and casinos responded with multiple decks.
Card games.Bridge: Bridge became a fashionable game in the 1920s and 30s, and Warren Buffett and Bill Gates are known to be avid players.
Card games.Rummy: Rummy players meld sets and runs, and the game is a parent of gin rummy and canasta, with roots probably in Mexico's conquian.
Card games.Solitaire: Solitaire, called Patience in Britain, is played alone, and its most popular form is Klondike, named for the gold rush.
Card games.Go Fish: Go Fish is a children's game in which players ask for matching cards, collecting sets of four.
Card games.Crazy Eights: Crazy Eights is the ancestor of Uno, where eights are wild and players try to dump their cards first.
Card games.Hearts: Hearts is a trick-taking game where you avoid points, and the queen of spades is worth 13 of them.
Card games.Spades: Spades is a partnership trick-taking game, invented in the 1930s in the United States, with spades always the trump suit.
Card games.Gin rummy: Gin rummy was invented around 1909 by a New York whist teacher, Elwood Baker, and was a craze in 1940s Hollywood.
Card games.Old Maid: Old Maid is a children's game in which the loser holds the unpaired queen, and the game is thought to date to Victorian times.
Card games.War: War is a game with no decisions at all: the higher card wins, so the result is decided by the deal.
Card games.Snap: Snap is a reflex game in Britain in which players shout when two matching cards appear.
Card games.Canasta: Canasta started in Uruguay in the 1940s and was a craze in the US in the 1950s, with melds of seven cards called canastas.
Card games.Mahjong: Mahjong uses tiles rather than cards, and it came from China in the 19th century and is played with 144 tiles.
Card games.Dominoes: Dominoes are tiles, not cards, and a double-six set has 28 pieces.
Card games.Yahtzee: Yahtzee uses five dice, not cards, and a roll of five matching dice scores 50 points.
Card games.Scrabble: Scrabble is a board game with 100 letter tiles, not a card game, though its tiles are made of wood or plastic.
Card games.Backgammon: Backgammon is a board game, not a card game, and relatives of it about 5,000 years old have been found in Iran.
Card games.Chess: Chess is a board game on 64 squares, not a card game, and a deck of cards has no pieces to move around.
Card games.Craps: Craps is a dice game played at a casino table, not a card game, and its name likely comes from an old word for a losing throw.
Card games.Roulette: Roulette means little wheel in French, and the story says Blaise Pascal's perpetual-motion experiments helped inspire the wheel.
Card games.Bingo: Bingo uses numbered cards but the cards are marked, not played, and the game is pure chance rather than a card game.
Card games.Jenga: Jenga is a stacking game of wooden blocks, played without a single card.

Rooms on the classic Clue board.Kitchen: The Kitchen is linked by a secret passage to the Study in the opposite corner. The game's British original, Cluedo, was patented by Anthony Pratt in 1947.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Ballroom: The Ballroom is one of the largest rooms on the board. It has no secret passage, so reaching it takes real dice rolls.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Conservatory: Its secret passage runs diagonally across the board to the Lounge, a handy shortcut for a suspect in a hurry.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Billiard Room: A billiard table was a fixture of British country houses, the world the UK original, Cluedo, was set in.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Library: The Library is where many players first guess, thanks to its classic murder-mystery feel. It has no secret passage.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Study: The Study's secret passage leads to the Kitchen in the far corner, letting you skip the dice roll.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Hall: Hall is one of the nine rooms you can name in a suggestion; the case file envelope, however, sits at the board's centre, not in any room.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Lounge: The Lounge's secret passage leads to the Conservatory, the opposite corner of the mansion.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Dining Room: The Dining Room is one of nine possible crime scenes. Like the Ballroom, it has no secret passage.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Bathroom: Not one of the nine rooms. A murder in the bath is classic Agatha Christie, but Clue keeps it to the public rooms.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Bedroom: Not a Clue room. All nine are public rooms where guests might gather, so nobody's private quarters appear.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Attic: Not on the board, which shows only the ground-floor rooms of the mansion.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Cellar: Not a room you can name in a suggestion. The sealed envelope holding the solution sits in the middle of the board instead.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Garage: No garage: the game's 1940s setting predates having a car stored inside a country house.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Nursery: No nursery on the board. Clue's rooms are all spaces for adult guests.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Pantry: Not on the board. Only the Kitchen represents the mansion's food areas.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Gym: Not on the board, which is based on a 1940s English country house, not a modern home.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Office: Not on the board; the Study covers the work-at-a-desk setting.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Laundry room: Not a Clue room. No domestic chore rooms appear in the mansion.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Game room: Not on the board. The Billiard Room is the closest thing the mansion has to a games room.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Basement: Not one of the nine rooms; the board shows only ground-level rooms.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Greenhouse: The Conservatory is the nearest thing: a glass-roofed room full of plants. A greenhouse isn't named.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Foyer: Not on the board. The Hall serves as the mansion's entrance.
Rooms on the classic Clue board.Garden: Not a room: the board shows only the mansion's interior, with no outdoor spaces at all.

Famous NHL players.Wayne Gretzky: The Great One holds over 60 NHL records, including 894 career goals, and wore number 99, which the league retired across all teams.
Famous NHL players.Mario Lemieux: The Penguins centre beat cancer in 1993 and came back to win a scoring title the same season; he later saved the club as its owner.
Famous NHL players.Sidney Crosby: Nicknamed Sid the Kid, he captained Pittsburgh to Stanley Cups and scored the golden goal for Canada at the 2010 Olympics in overtime.
Famous NHL players.Alexander Ovechkin: The Russian winger passed Gretzky's record for career goals in 2025, and is famous for his one-timer from the left circle.
Famous NHL players.Bobby Orr: The Bruins defenceman won the scoring title twice as a defender, which no one else has done, and his flying goal in 1970 is iconic.
Famous NHL players.Gordie Howe: Mr. Hockey played in five different decades, finishing up at age 52, and the Gordie Howe hat trick is a goal, an assist and a fight.
Famous NHL players.Connor McDavid: The Oilers captain is so fast that he skates with the puck faster than most skate without it, and has won several scoring titles.
Famous NHL players.Mark Messier: The only player to captain two different teams to a Stanley Cup, he famously guaranteed a win in 1994 and delivered a hat trick.
Famous NHL players.Jaromir Jagr: A Czech winger who kept playing professionally into his fifties, he is second only to Gretzky in career points, and his mullet is legendary.
Famous NHL players.Patrick Roy: The goalie pioneered the butterfly style and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP three times, at ages 20 to 35.
Famous NHL players.Maurice Richard: The Rocket was the first NHL player to score 50 goals in a season, in 50 games, and a 1955 suspension of him led to the Richard Riot.
Famous NHL players.Martin Brodeur: The goalie holds the NHL records for wins and shutouts, and he even scored goals himself, shooting into empty nets.
Famous NHL players.Tom Brady: Winner of seven Super Bowls, he played American football, not hockey, and was famously drafted 199th overall in 2000.
Famous NHL players.Michael Jordan: He won six NBA titles with the Bulls, and he famously tried baseball in between. Never an NHL player, though.
Famous NHL players.Babe Ruth: Baseball's Sultan of Swat started out as a pitcher for Boston, and holds no place in a list of NHL stars.
Famous NHL players.Derek Jeter: The long-time Yankees captain won five World Series and collected over 3,000 hits; his sport is baseball.
Famous NHL players.Kobe Bryant: He spent all 20 NBA seasons with the Lakers and scored 81 points in a game in 2006, in basketball rather than hockey.
Famous NHL players.Peyton Manning: A quarterback who won a Super Bowl with both the Colts and the Broncos, and holds a list of NFL passing records.
Famous NHL players.Shaquille O'Neal: At about seven feet, he won four NBA titles; he has a rapping and acting career, but never played hockey.
Famous NHL players.Tiger Woods: The golfer won the Masters at 21 by a record 12 strokes, and has 15 major titles, not any Stanley Cups.
Famous NHL players.Joe Montana: Four Super Bowl wins without an interception in any of them, with a famous clutch drive in the 1989 game for San Francisco.
Famous NHL players.LeBron James: The NBA's all-time leading scorer, passing Kareem Abdul-Jabbar in 2023, plays basketball, not hockey.
Famous NHL players.Hank Aaron: He hit 755 home runs, the record for 33 years until 2007, and endured terrible abuse while chasing Ruth's mark.
Famous NHL players.Jerry Rice: The 49ers receiver holds NFL records for receptions, touchdowns and receiving yards, and played football, not ice hockey.

Track and field stars.Usain Bolt: The Jamaican sprinter holds the 100 m record, 9.58 s, and 200 m record, 19.19 s, both set at the 2009 Berlin Worlds.
Track and field stars.Carl Lewis: He won nine Olympic gold medals, in sprints and long jump, and took the long jump gold at four consecutive Games from 1984 to 1996.
Track and field stars.Jesse Owens: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics he won four gold medals, a powerful rebuttal to the host nation's propaganda about racial superiority.
Track and field stars.Flo-Jo: Florence Griffith Joyner still holds the 100 m and 200 m women's world records from 1988, and she was known for flamboyant one-legged running suits.
Track and field stars.Mo Farah: The Somali-born runner won double Olympic gold in the 5,000 and 10,000 m at London 2012 and again at Rio 2016, striking his Mobot pose.
Track and field stars.Eliud Kipchoge: In 2019 he ran a marathon in under two hours, 1:59:40, in a special event, and he holds multiple official world records.
Track and field stars.Michael Johnson: He won the 200 and 400 metres at the 1996 Olympics, with a famous upright running style and gold shoes.
Track and field stars.Sebastian Coe: The British middle-distance runner won 1500 m gold at two Olympics in a row, and later led the organisation of London 2012.
Track and field stars.Allyson Felix: The American sprinter won more Olympic medals than any other track athlete, with 11, including seven golds.
Track and field stars.Haile Gebrselassie: The Ethiopian distance great set 27 world records, and his big smile through marathons is almost as famous as his speed.
Track and field stars.Paula Radcliffe: The British runner set a marathon world record of 2:15:25 in 2003, one that stood for 16 years.
Track and field stars.Edwin Moses: The hurdler won 122 consecutive races over nearly ten years, from 1977 to 1987, taking exactly 13 strides between hurdles.
Track and field stars.Michael Phelps: The most decorated Olympian ever, with 28 medals, 23 of them gold, but he's a swimmer, not a track athlete.
Track and field stars.Mark Spitz: He won seven golds at Munich 1972, all in world-record time, in the swimming pool.
Track and field stars.Simone Biles: A gymnast with more World Championship medals than any other gymnast, and she's one of the best in the sport.
Track and field stars.Nadia Comaneci: At 14, in 1976, she scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics, so the scoreboard had to show 1.00 as it couldn't show ten.
Track and field stars.Katie Ledecky: An American swimmer who dominates distance freestyle, and she holds world records in the 800 and 1500 metres.
Track and field stars.Ian Thorpe: The Thorpedo was an Australian swimmer famous for his size 17 feet, and he won five Olympic golds in the pool.
Track and field stars.Chris Hoy: A Scottish track cyclist with six Olympic golds, the velodrome was his arena, and he was later knighted.
Track and field stars.Bradley Wiggins: He won the 2012 Tour de France and an Olympic gold a few weeks later, but he's a cyclist.
Track and field stars.Steve Redgrave: A British rower with five straight Olympic golds from 1984 to 2000, and he sat in a boat, not on the track.
Track and field stars.Shaun White: The Flying Tomato is a snowboarder and skateboarder with three Olympic golds in the halfpipe.
Track and field stars.Greg Louganis: A diver who won double golds in two Olympics, and he famously hit his head on the board in 1988 and still won.
Track and field stars.Tom Daley: He first competed at the Olympics at 14 and won gold in the 10m synchro in 2021, a diver who also loves knitting.

Aztec or Maya gods.Quetzalcoatl: The Feathered Serpent of the Aztecs was a creator and wind god; legend says he sailed east promising to return.
Aztec or Maya gods.Tlaloc: Aztec rain god received child sacrifices at Tenochtitlan's Great Temple, which he shared with Huitzilopochtli.
Aztec or Maya gods.Huitzilopochtli: Aztec war and sun god, his name means 'Hummingbird of the South'; his twin temple towered over Tenochtitlan.
Aztec or Maya gods.Tezcatlipoca: His name means 'Smoking Mirror'; this Aztec god of night and fate had an obsidian mirror and lost a foot to the earth monster.
Aztec or Maya gods.Kukulkan: The Maya Feathered Serpent; at Chichen Itza, equinox shadows seem to slither down the pyramid's stairs as a snake.
Aztec or Maya gods.Itzamna: Maya creator god and patron of writing and medicine, he was often shown as a wise old man.
Aztec or Maya gods.Chaac: Maya rain god with a long, curling nose, who swings a lightning axe; Uxmal's Palace of the Masks is covered in his faces.
Aztec or Maya gods.Xochiquetzal: Aztec goddess of flowers, beauty and love, she was also patron of artists and weavers.
Aztec or Maya gods.Mictlantecuhtli: Aztec lord of the dead, usually shown as a skeleton, ruled Mictlan, a nine-level underworld the dead crossed over four years.
Aztec or Maya gods.Coatlicue: Her name means 'Serpent Skirt'; the Aztec earth goddess gave birth to Huitzilopochtli, and her giant statue was unearthed in Mexico City in 1790.
Aztec or Maya gods.Ixchel: Maya goddess of the moon, weaving, medicine and childbirth, she was often shown with a rabbit; Cozumel was her pilgrimage site.
Aztec or Maya gods.Xipe Totec: Aztec god of spring and renewal; priests wore flayed skins in his honor, to echo the earth shedding its old growth.
Aztec or Maya gods.Ra: A trap: Ra is the Egyptian sun god, not Mesoamerican. Mesoamerican counterparts like Tonatiuh and Huitzilopochtli also ruled the sun.
Aztec or Maya gods.Thor: The Norse thunder god. Thunder in Maya belief was Chaac's work, and Aztec storms belonged to Tlaloc.
Aztec or Maya gods.Zeus: King of the Greek gods, who hurled lightning; the Aztec and Maya had no single ruler of heaven like him.
Aztec or Maya gods.Inti: Inti is Inca, not Aztec or Maya; the Inca emperors claimed to descend from this sun god.
Aztec or Maya gods.Viracocha: An Inca creator god who rose from Lake Titicaca; the Aztecs and Maya never knew him, as the Andes are a world apart.
Aztec or Maya gods.Pachamama: Pachamama, Andean Mother Earth, is Inca-era South American, and still receives offerings in the Andes today.
Aztec or Maya gods.Amaterasu: Japan's sun goddess hid in a cave, plunging the world into darkness until a noisy party lured her out.
Aztec or Maya gods.Anubis: Jackal-headed Egyptian god of embalming, who weighed hearts of the dead against a feather.
Aztec or Maya gods.Odin: Norse chief god, who gave an eye for wisdom and hung nine nights on a tree to learn the runes.
Aztec or Maya gods.Marduk: The patron god of Babylon rose to chief of the gods after defeating Tiamat in the Enuma Elish.
Aztec or Maya gods.Osiris: The Egyptian lord of the dead was murdered by Set, then resurrected by Isis; he ruled the underworld.
Aztec or Maya gods.Hera: Greek queen of the gods and goddess of marriage; the Aztec and Maya had their own divine couples elsewhere, like Ometeotl.

Things a Roman emperor might wear.Toga: A draped wool garment that marked a Roman citizen. Emperors wore a toga picta, richly embroidered, on state occasions.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Laurel wreath: A wreath of bay leaves worn as a sign of victory and rank. Julius Caesar was said to wear his partly to hide his baldness.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Tunic: The everyday Roman garment worn by all classes, usually worn beneath other clothes. Senators' tunics had a wide purple stripe.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Sandals: Roman footwear, leather with thongs. Emperor Caligula's nickname 'little boots' came from a small military sandal-like boot, caliga.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Purple cloak: Tyrian purple dye came from sea snails, taking thousands of them to colour one garment. Under later emperors, it was reserved for them.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Signet ring: Used to seal documents with a personal stamp in wax. Passing it on was how a Roman ruler signalled his successor.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Cuirass: A sculpted breastplate shaped like a muscular torso, worn by generals and emperors to show military might. Augustus appears in one at Prima Porta.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Brooch: A decorative pin that held cloaks in place at the shoulder. Fancy ones, often in gold, signalled rank.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Leather belt: A belt, a sign of military service. Roman soldiers wore decorative ones to carry daggers and show rank.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Top hat: Trap: a tall silk hat of the 1800s, worn by gentlemen over a thousand years after Rome's emperors.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Kimono: Trap: Japan's traditional robe, tied with an obi sash. Rome and Japan never met in antiquity.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Ruff collar: Trap: a stiff pleated collar from 16th-century Europe, a thousand years after Rome fell.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Powdered wig: Trap: powdered wigs were fashionable in the 1600s and 1700s, long after Rome.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Monocle: Trap: a single eyeglass lens, a fashion of the 1800s. Romans had no such thing as eyeglasses.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Pith helmet: Trap: a lightweight sun helmet worn by explorers and colonial officials in the 1800s.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Kilt: Trap: Scottish men's pleated skirt, with Roman soldiers known to scorn the Celts who wore trousers.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Tricorn hat: Trap: a three-cornered hat popular in the 1700s, centuries after Rome had fallen.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Wristwatch: Trap: Romans told time with sundials and water clocks, and wristwatches arrived around 1900.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Cufflinks: Trap: cufflinks fasten shirt cuffs, which only developed in later centuries. Romans used brooches and belts.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Beret: Trap: a soft round cap associated with France and the Basque country, not with the Roman court.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Fedora: Trap: a soft felt hat that appeared in the 1880s. No Roman emperor wore one.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Bowler hat: Trap: a round felt hat designed in London in 1849, far later than any Roman emperor.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Sombrero: Trap: a wide-brimmed hat from Mexico, with a name meaning 'shade', and unknown in the Roman world.
Things a Roman emperor might wear.Bow tie: Trap: neckwear that grew popular in the late 1800s, long after the Roman Empire had vanished.

Things with antennas.Radio: A radio's antenna picks up radio waves, and the telescopic metal rod on a pocket radio is just a length of wire.
Things with antennas.Walkie-talkie: The walkie-talkie was developed during the Second World War, and its stubby antenna sends and receives radio signals.
Things with antennas.Ant: Ants use their antennae to smell, touch and communicate, tapping each other to trade information about food.
Things with antennas.Butterfly: Butterflies have club-tipped antennae while moths usually have feathery or plain ones, a handy way to tell them apart.
Things with antennas.Cockroach: A cockroach's antennae can be longer than its body, and they sense touch, smell and air movement all at once.
Things with antennas.Wi-Fi router: Many routers hide their antennas inside, but they send and receive signals in the 2.4 and 5 gigahertz bands.
Things with antennas.Satellite: A satellite uses antennas, including dish ones, to receive instructions and send data to Earth.
Things with antennas.Lobster: Lobsters have two pairs of antennae, long ones for touch and short ones for smell.
Things with antennas.Bee: A bee's antennae smell and feel, and they can detect flower scents and even the electric field around a flower.
Things with antennas.Cell tower: Cell towers carry antennae at the top to broadcast phone signals across the area around them.
Things with antennas.Old TV set: Rabbit ears antennas on old TVs were adjusted by hand, and people often wrapped foil on them to improve the picture.
Things with antennas.Spider: Spiders have no antennae; they sense the world through sensitive hairs and small leg-like pedipalps.
Things with antennas.Scorpion: Scorpions do not have antennae; they detect vibrations through their legs and pectines on the belly.
Things with antennas.Worm: Earthworms have no antennae and no eyes, but they feel light and vibrations with skin cells.
Things with antennas.Snake: A snake flicks its forked tongue to taste the air, doing the job that antennae do for insects.
Things with antennas.Fish: Catfish have whisker-like barbels for taste and touch, but they are not antennae.
Things with antennas.Toaster: A toaster has heating wires, not antennae, because it never needs to receive or send signals.
Things with antennas.Kettle: A kettle just boils water and needs no signal, so it needs no antenna.
Things with antennas.Lamp: A simple lamp has a bulb and a wire, and no antenna for sending or receiving anything.
Things with antennas.Book: A book has paper and ink and no antennas, though a few books now come with e-ink screens.
Things with antennas.Candle: A candle burns wax with a wick and has nothing to do with signals.
Things with antennas.Bird: Birds sense with eyes, ears and beaks, with no antennae, but some can sense magnetic fields.
Things with antennas.Octopus: An octopus has eight arms and sensitive suckers, but no antennae; those belong to insects and crustaceans.
Things with antennas.Cat: A cat's whiskers are sensitive touch tools, but whiskers are not antennae.

Things on a car dashboard.Speedometer: Modern speedometers read a few percent high on purpose, because makers must avoid ever showing less than your true speed.
Things on a car dashboard.Fuel gauge: A small arrow next to the pump icon shows which side the fuel door is on, a feature found on many cars.
Things on a car dashboard.Odometer: Rolling back an odometer is a crime in many countries, but older mechanical ones were easy to alter.
Things on a car dashboard.Tachometer: The rev counter shows engine revolutions per minute, and the 'redline' marks the speed past which the engine risks damage.
Things on a car dashboard.Warning lights: Every light comes on briefly at startup as a bulb check, and a flashing check-engine light means a serious misfire.
Things on a car dashboard.Temperature gauge: The needle should sit in the middle, and if it climbs to the red the engine is overheating and needs to stop.
Things on a car dashboard.Air vents: Round vents became the standard of many dashboards, and the louvers let you direct air at your face or feet.
Things on a car dashboard.Car radio: The first commercial car radio was Motorola's in 1930, and it was so costly it added up to a quarter of a car's price.
Things on a car dashboard.Hazard light button: The red triangle flashes all four indicators, and in many countries it is used when stopped or in traffic jams.
Things on a car dashboard.Clock: A dashboard clock is there to help, though the first car clocks were mechanical and wound by hand.
Things on a car dashboard.Handbrake: The parking brake lever sits between seats or under the dash, and it works on the rear wheels by cable.
Things on a car dashboard.Brake pedal: The pedal is on the floor, which is why a dashboard is above, never below, your feet.
Things on a car dashboard.Sunroof: The sunroof is a panel in the roof, and has nothing to do with the dash at the front.
Things on a car dashboard.Seat belt: Volvo's Nils Bohlin invented the modern three-point belt in 1959, and Volvo gave away the patent freely.
Things on a car dashboard.Headrest: The headrest protects your neck in a rear-end crash, and it attaches to the seat, not the dash.
Things on a car dashboard.Trunk: The trunk is at the rear, and in British English it is a boot.
Things on a car dashboard.Spare tire: Many modern cars skip a full spare and carry a repair kit instead, saving weight and fuel.
Things on a car dashboard.Exhaust pipe: The exhaust runs below and out the back, and the dashboard is up front in the cabin.
Things on a car dashboard.Windshield wiper: Mary Anderson patented the wiper in 1903 after a snowy trip, and the blades sit outside the glass, not on the dashboard.
Things on a car dashboard.License plate: Plates are on the bumper, and the first plate for cars in France dates from 1901.
Things on a car dashboard.Hubcap: Hubcaps cover the wheel center and fit on the outside of the vehicle, not within the dashboard.
Things on a car dashboard.Mud flap: The flap hangs behind the tire to stop mud and stones thrown at other cars.
Things on a car dashboard.Roof rack: The roof rack sits atop the car for luggage, and has no relationship to the dash.
Things on a car dashboard.Tow bar: The tow bar is bolted to the chassis at the rear and is rated for a maximum trailer weight.

Real medical conditions.Tinnitus: Tinnitus is hearing ringing or buzzing with no outside source, and it affects a sizable share of adults.
Real medical conditions.Vertigo: Vertigo is the false sense that the world is spinning, a symptom rather than a fear of heights.
Real medical conditions.Gout: Gout comes from uric acid crystals, often striking the big toe, and was once nicknamed the disease of kings.
Real medical conditions.Rickets: Rickets softens children's bones from too little vitamin D, and fortified milk helped nearly wipe it out.
Real medical conditions.Scurvy: Scurvy is a vitamin C shortage that killed huge numbers of sailors until citrus became a standard remedy.
Real medical conditions.Shingles: Shingles is the chickenpox virus waking up decades later, and a vaccine can cut the risk considerably.
Real medical conditions.Croup: Croup gives children a barking, seal-like cough because an infection swells the airway below the vocal cords.
Real medical conditions.Hives: Hives are itchy welts, and each one usually fades within a day while new ones appear elsewhere.
Real medical conditions.Bunions: A bunion is a bump at the base of the big toe, caused by the joint shifting out of alignment.
Real medical conditions.Sciatica: Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve, the body's longest, which runs from the lower back down each leg.
Real medical conditions.Halitosis: Halitosis is the clinical word for bad breath, and most cases start with bacteria on the tongue.
Real medical conditions.Rosacea: Rosacea causes facial redness and bumps, and has been nicknamed the 'curse of the Celts'.
Real medical conditions.Clematis: A climbing flowering vine, not an illness, though its name sounds clinical.
Real medical conditions.Hypotenuse: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle; the medical word that sounds like it is hypotension.
Real medical conditions.Rhombus: A rhombus is a four-sided shape with equal sides, so it sounds medical but belongs to geometry.
Real medical conditions.Croissant: Its name means 'crescent' in French, and the pastry is a bakery item rather than any ailment.
Real medical conditions.Fettuccine: Fettuccine means 'little ribbons' in Italian, and it is a pasta, not a condition.
Real medical conditions.Stalactite: Stalactites hang from a cave ceiling, built from mineral drips over centuries; they are rock, not illness.
Real medical conditions.Tinsel: Tinsel is shiny decoration, and it echoes tinnitus only by sound.
Real medical conditions.Verbena: Verbena is a flowering plant; the herb called lemon verbena is a different plant from a related family.
Real medical conditions.Gnocchi: Gnocchi are Italian dumplings, often made from potato, and the 'gn' is pronounced like 'ny'.
Real medical conditions.Calamari: Calamari is Italian for squid, usually served as rings fried in batter.
Real medical conditions.Bruschetta: Bruschetta is grilled bread rubbed with garlic, pronounced with a hard k: broo-SKET-ah.
Real medical conditions.Piccolo: A piccolo is a tiny flute pitched an octave above the standard flute; 'piccolo' means 'small' in Italian.

Things that have a shell.Turtle: A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton, fused to the ribs and spine, so it can never crawl out of it like a hermit crab.
Things that have a shell.Snail: A snail's shell grows with it in a spiral, and the animal can pull its whole body inside to survive dry spells for months.
Things that have a shell.Egg: An eggshell is covered in thousands of tiny pores, letting the developing chick breathe through what looks like a solid wall.
Things that have a shell.Crab: Crabs outgrow their shells and shed them in a process called molting, hiding while the new shell hardens.
Things that have a shell.Clam: Some clams live for centuries; an ocean quahog nicknamed Ming was about 500 years old when scientists found it.
Things that have a shell.Oyster: An oyster can switch sex during its life, and a single one filters tens of liters of water through its shell each day.
Things that have a shell.Peanut: Peanut shells are the pod of a plant that ripens underground, and botanically peanuts are legumes, closer to beans than nuts.
Things that have a shell.Walnut: A walnut shell is so hard that it is ground up and used for polishing metal and cleaning jet engines.
Things that have a shell.Lobster: Lobsters are red only after cooking; alive, their shells are usually a dark mottled blue-green or brown.
Things that have a shell.Tortoise: A tortoise's dome-shaped shell is built for defense on land; some giant tortoises live well past 150 years.
Things that have a shell.Coconut: A coconut has a hard woody shell, and the three 'eyes' at one end are where the sprout will emerge, so it counts as a seed.
Things that have a shell.Pistachio: Pistachio shells split open on their own as the nut ripens, and the crack is why the nut is nicknamed the smiling or happy nut.
Things that have a shell.Taco: A hard taco shell is a fried tortilla bent into a U, so this is the odd one out: a shell you can eat.
Things that have a shell.Slug: A slug is essentially a snail that gave up its shell; some species keep a tiny plate of shell hidden under the skin.
Things that have a shell.Earthworm: Earthworms have no shell or bones at all; they move with muscles and bristles, and can breathe through their skin.
Things that have a shell.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are about 95 percent water and have no shell, bones, or brain; they have drifted the seas for over 500 million years.
Things that have a shell.Octopus: An octopus has no shell, so it can squeeze through any gap larger than its hard beak, a trick that helps it escape tanks.
Things that have a shell.Banana: A banana has a peel, not a shell, and the plant is technically a giant herb; botanically its fruit is a berry.
Things that have a shell.Frog: Frogs have no shell, but their moist skin absorbs water and oxygen, so they usually do not need to drink.
Things that have a shell.Lizard: Lizards wear scales, not shells, and many can drop their tails to escape a predator, then grow a replacement.
Things that have a shell.Grape: Grapes have only a thin skin, and the dusty white film on it is natural yeast-rich bloom, which is how wine starts fermenting.
Things that have a shell.Mushroom: The mushroom you see is just the fruiting body; the real organism is a hidden web of threads that can span acres.
Things that have a shell.Starfish: Starfish have a bumpy spiny skin, not a shell, and can regrow a lost arm; they are now called sea stars since they are not fish.
Things that have a shell.Eel: Eels are slimy, scaleless fish with no shell, and European eels travel thousands of kilometers to breed in the Sargasso Sea.

Terrible at hide and seek.Elephant: An elephant weighs several tonnes and is hard to hide, yet it can walk almost silently, thanks to the cushion of fat in its feet.
Terrible at hide and seek.Giraffe: A giraffe stands up to about 5.5 meters tall, taller than most trees on the savanna, so there is nowhere to tuck its neck.
Terrible at hide and seek.Fire truck: A fire truck is bright red or yellow, with flashing lights and a siren, so hiding is clearly not its job.
Terrible at hide and seek.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon is huge and brightly colored, and visible from kilometers away, which makes it a poor hider.
Terrible at hide and seek.Lighthouse: A lighthouse exists to be seen, with a tall tower and a powerful beam that carries tens of kilometers over the sea.
Terrible at hide and seek.Marching band: A marching band is loud, uniformed, and moving in formation, so seekers can hear it from blocks away.
Terrible at hide and seek.Blue whale: A blue whale is up to 30 meters long, and its call is so loud that it can be heard hundreds of kilometers away.
Terrible at hide and seek.Skyscraper: A skyscraper towers over everything, and the tallest, the Burj Khalifa, is over 800 meters tall.
Terrible at hide and seek.Ferris wheel: A Ferris wheel is a huge rotating wheel in the middle of a fairground, so it can't be missed from anywhere.
Terrible at hide and seek.Peacock: A peacock's tail has about 200 feathers and eyespots, which make it easy to spot, and are made to be.
Terrible at hide and seek.Flamingo: Flamingos are bright pink from carotenoid pigments in their food, and they live in huge flocks that are easy to spot.
Terrible at hide and seek.Chameleon: Chameleons are great at hiding, though color change is mainly for communication and temperature, not just camouflage.
Terrible at hide and seek.Octopus: An octopus can change color and texture in a fraction of a second, even though it is thought to be colorblind.
Terrible at hide and seek.Stick insect: A stick insect looks so much like a twig that it will even sway as if in the wind to avoid detection.
Terrible at hide and seek.Mouse: A mouse is small enough to squeeze through a gap the size of a pencil's width and hide almost anywhere.
Terrible at hide and seek.Ant: An ant is tiny and can hide in almost any crack, and a colony can have millions of members.
Terrible at hide and seek.Snowshoe hare: A snowshoe hare molts to white fur in winter to match the snow and turns brown again in summer, so it hides well.
Terrible at hide and seek.Leaf insect: A leaf insect looks like a leaf, with veins and even chew marks, and its eggs resemble seeds.
Terrible at hide and seek.Flounder: A flounder lies flat on the seabed and can change color to match the sand, with both eyes on one side of the head.
Terrible at hide and seek.Ninja: Ninjas were the covert agents of feudal Japan, famed for stealth and for the dark clothing that was probably a stage invention.
Terrible at hide and seek.Snow leopard: The snow leopard's gray, spotted coat blends into mountain rock so well that it is called the ghost of the mountains.
Terrible at hide and seek.Cuttlefish: A cuttlefish changes its skin color and pattern in a flash to vanish or hypnotize prey, and it has W-shaped pupils.
Terrible at hide and seek.Owl: An owl's mottled feathers match tree bark, and its feathers also silence its flight so that prey hears nothing.
Terrible at hide and seek.Arctic fox: An arctic fox turns white in winter and brownish in summer, so it blends into the tundra all year.

Farm animals.Cow: Cows have a best friend, and they can show stress when separated, and spend most of the day chewing cud.
Farm animals.Pig: Pigs are among the smartest animals, and can learn to play simple video games, with a joystick.
Farm animals.Sheep: Sheep can recognize individual faces, and studies suggest they remember them for years.
Farm animals.Goat: Goats were among the first animals domesticated, more than 10,000 years ago.
Farm animals.Chicken: Chickens outnumber humans on Earth, with about 25 billion alive at any time.
Farm animals.Horse: Horses can sleep standing up, thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs.
Farm animals.Duck: A duck's quack does echo, despite the old myth, though it can be hard to notice because the sound is brief and fades fast.
Farm animals.Turkey: Wild turkeys can fly short distances and run fast, and Benjamin Franklin admired them.
Farm animals.Donkey: Donkeys have a famously strong bond and can remember places and friends for decades.
Farm animals.Goose: Geese mate for life and are fiercely protective, and have been used as guard animals in some places.
Farm animals.Rooster: A rooster crows at dawn thanks to a body clock, and it can crow at any time of day, too.
Farm animals.Wolf: A wolf is wild, and domestic dogs descend from wolves, though not any farm animal does.
Farm animals.Giraffe: Giraffes are African wildlife, and their necks have just seven vertebrae, the same as ours.
Farm animals.Fox: Foxes are wild, and the red fox is the most widely spread wild carnivore on Earth.
Farm animals.Zebra: Zebras are wild, and each has a unique stripe pattern, like a fingerprint.
Farm animals.Moose: Moose are the largest deer, and wild, and can stand about six feet at the shoulder.
Farm animals.Raccoon: Raccoons are wild, and they famously dunk food in water, because their paws are very sensitive.
