Farm animals.Squirrel: Squirrels are wild, and they forget where they bury many of their nuts, which helps plant new trees.
Farm animals.Kangaroo: Kangaroos are wild Australian animals, and they can't walk backward.
Farm animals.Lion: Lions are wild big cats, and the only cats that live in social groups called prides.
Farm animals.Bear: Bears are wild, and they can smell food from miles away.
Farm animals.Badger: Badgers are wild, and they build large underground burrows called setts that can last for generations.
Farm animals.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs are wild, and have about 5,000 to 7,000 spines.
Farm animals.Skunk: Skunks are wild, and can spray their musk accurately up to about ten feet.

Tools for measuring.Tape measure: A tape measure's metal blade curves slightly, which keeps it rigid when extended and lets it coil neatly back.
Tools for measuring.Ruler: Rulers have been used for thousands of years, and the Indus Valley civilization used marked ivory rods.
Tools for measuring.Spirit level: The spirit level's bubble in a vial of liquid was invented in the 17th century by Melchisedech Thevenot.
Tools for measuring.Calipers: Calipers measure the distance between two sides of an object, and vernier versions can read to fractions of a millimeter.
Tools for measuring.Protractor: A protractor measures angles in degrees, and a full circle has 360, a number from ancient Babylon.
Tools for measuring.Thermometer: Galileo built an early thermometer around 1600, and Fahrenheit's mercury version came about in 1714.
Tools for measuring.Weighing scale: A weighing scale compares an object's weight against a spring or known masses. Balances measure mass, not weight.
Tools for measuring.Stopwatch: A stopwatch measures elapsed time, and modern ones in sports can be accurate to a thousandth of a second.
Tools for measuring.Micrometer: A micrometer uses a precise screw thread to measure tiny distances, down to a hundredth of a millimeter or better.
Tools for measuring.Measuring jug: A measuring jug shows volume in marked lines, which lets you follow a recipe's cups and milliliters.
Tools for measuring.Odometer: An odometer counts how far a vehicle has traveled, and the Roman architect Vitruvius described one in wheels of a cart.
Tools for measuring.Barometer: A barometer measures air pressure. Torricelli made the first one in 1643 using mercury, and falling pressure often means rain.
Tools for measuring.Anemometer: An anemometer measures wind speed with spinning cups, an idea first sketched in the 15th century.
Tools for measuring.Hammer: A hammer drives or strikes things such as nails, so it's for building and doesn't measure anything.
Tools for measuring.Chisel: A chisel carves wood or stone, so it's a shaping tool, not a measuring one, and needs a mallet.
Tools for measuring.Screwdriver: A screwdriver turns screws, so it's an assembly tool, and it measures nothing at all in the workshop.
Tools for measuring.Pliers: Pliers grip and bend things such as wire. They have no scale and measure nothing at all, so they're out.
Tools for measuring.Wrench: A wrench turns bolts and nuts, so it's a tool for tightening and loosening, not for measuring.
Tools for measuring.Whisk: A whisk beats eggs and cream in the kitchen. It's a kitchen tool and measures nothing at all.
Tools for measuring.Saw: A saw cuts wood, and carpenters use it after measuring, not to measure, so it doesn't fit this list.
Tools for measuring.Shovel: A shovel digs holes, so it's a garden tool and not a measuring tool, however deep it goes.
Tools for measuring.Rake: A rake gathers leaves and smooths soil, so it's a garden tool and measures nothing at all.
Tools for measuring.Paintbrush: A paintbrush applies paint and measures nothing, though artists use it alongside a ruler or a tape.
Tools for measuring.Stapler: A stapler fastens sheets of paper and measures nothing, so it doesn't belong with the rulers.

Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Enter: On typewriters, the carriage return key physically slid the carriage back, and Enter inherited its job.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Shift: The name comes from typewriters, where pressing it shifted the whole carriage so the other half of a key's characters would print.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Tab: Short for tabulator: it comes from typewriters that jumped to preset columns for tables.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Escape: The Escape key dates back to 1960s computers, where it was originally used to signal a change in meaning for what followed.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Backspace: On a typewriter it only moved the carriage back, but on a computer it erases the character to the left.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Caps Lock: Descended from the typewriter's shift lock, which held the whole carriage up.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Delete: Delete removes the character to the right of the cursor, while Backspace erases to the left.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Home: Jumps the cursor to the start of the line, and some programs use it to go to the top of a document.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.End: Jumps to the end of a line, and with Ctrl it goes to the end of a document.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Page Up: Scrolls up one screenful, and it is a quick way to move through long documents.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Insert: Toggles between inserting and overwriting text, which a lot of people hit by accident.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Spacebar: It's the biggest key on the keyboard, because thumbs hit it constantly, and it is the only one that most typists press with a thumb.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Alt: Short for alternate, and Alt codes can type characters not on the keyboard, such as holding Alt and typing numbers.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Ctrl: The Control key modifies other keys, and its shortcuts like Ctrl+C are among the most used in computing.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Turbo: The turbo button was on 1990s PCs to switch speed, and yes, it actually slowed the computer down.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Undo: Ctrl+Z is the undo shortcut, but there's no dedicated key for it on standard keyboards.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Copy: Copy is a shortcut, Ctrl+C, rather than a key, though old Sun keyboards had dedicated copy keys.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Paste: You paste with Ctrl+V, a shortcut chosen so that it sits next to X and C on the keyboard.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Save: Save is a shortcut, Ctrl+S, and the floppy disk icon still represents it despite floppies being long gone.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Reboot: No keyboard has a reboot key, though a classic shortcut was Ctrl+Alt+Delete.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Like: Likes belong to social media, not the keyboard.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Shutdown: Not a key on a standard keyboard, though some have a sleep or power key.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Send: Email programs have a Send button, but keyboards don't have one.
Keys on a standard computer keyboard.Download: Downloading is something your computer does, not a key on the keyboard.

Video file extensions..mp4: MP4 is the most widely supported video format, and it's built on Apple's QuickTime container design.
Video file extensions..mov: This is Apple's QuickTime format, and it's common for iPhone and professional video.
Video file extensions..avi: AVI came from Microsoft in 1992 and is an old container that is less efficient than modern formats.
Video file extensions..mkv: Matroska is an open container that can hold unlimited audio, video and subtitle tracks, and its name comes from a Russian word for nesting doll.
Video file extensions..wmv: Windows Media Video was Microsoft's own format, widely used in the 2000s.
Video file extensions..flv: Flash Video powered early YouTube before Flash was retired in 2020.
Video file extensions..webm: WebM is an open format from Google designed for the web, which uses VP8 or VP9 video.
Video file extensions..m4v: This is Apple's variant of MP4, used by iTunes for videos, sometimes with copy protection.
Video file extensions..mpeg: MPEG stands for the Moving Picture Experts Group, which sets many standards for video and audio.
Video file extensions..mp3: MP3 is an audio format, not video, and it famously compresses music to a tenth of its size.
Video file extensions..wav: WAV is uncompressed audio from Microsoft and IBM, so its files are large.
Video file extensions..jpg: JPG is an image format; its compression discards details people rarely notice.
Video file extensions..png: PNG is a lossless image format with transparency, created as a free alternative to GIF.
Video file extensions..gif: GIFs are images that can loop short animations, but they're not designed for real video and have only 256 colors.
Video file extensions..pdf: PDF is a document format invented by Adobe in the early 1990s to look the same anywhere.
Video file extensions..docx: DOCX is a Word document, which is actually a zipped bundle of XML files.
Video file extensions..txt: TXT holds plain text only, and it's the simplest document format.
Video file extensions..zip: ZIP is a compressed archive that can contain any files, including videos.
Video file extensions..exe: EXE is an executable program on Windows, not a video.
Video file extensions..flac: FLAC is lossless audio, meaning no sound quality is lost when compressed.
Video file extensions..psd: PSD is Photoshop's layered image format, not a video.
Video file extensions..html: HTML is the markup of web pages, though pages can embed videos.
Video file extensions..csv: CSV stores spreadsheet data as plain text separated by commas.
Video file extensions..ppt: PPT is the older PowerPoint presentation format, which can include video but isn't one.

Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Power Pellet: Eating one of the four big pellets turns the ghosts blue for a few seconds, letting you chomp them for escalating points up to 1,600 per pellet.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Blinky: The red ghost, nicknamed Shadow, tails Pac-Man directly and gets faster once only a few dots remain, which is the Cruise Elroy mode.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Pinky: Nicknamed Speedy, this pink ghost aims at a spot ahead of Pac-Man's mouth, so reversing direction is a classic way to shake it.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Inky: Nicknamed Bashful, the cyan ghost uses both Pac-Man's position and Blinky's to decide where to go, making him the least predictable.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Clyde: Nicknamed Pokey, the orange ghost chases when far away but wanders off to his corner when he gets close, as if losing his nerve.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Cherry: The first bonus fruit, appearing on level one for 100 points; the fruit rotates through a fixed list as levels climb.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Strawberry: The level-two bonus is worth 300 points, a small step up in a ladder of bonuses that ends with a key worth 5,000.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Orange: Oranges appear on levels three and four for 500 points, part of a fruit parade that gets richer as the game progresses.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Bell: A 3,000 point bonus that shows up around level nine, one of the few bonus items that isn't a fruit.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Key: The final bonus item, worth 5,000 points, sits permanently from level 13 onward, as the game never changes it again.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Galaxian: Taken from another Namco arcade hit, this spaceship is a 2,000 point bonus, and a rare crossover in early arcade design.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Apple: Apples worth 700 points show up on levels five and six, midway through the original game's fruit ladder.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Melon: A watermelon-like melon is worth 1,000 points, and appears at levels seven and eight before the Galaxian takes over.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Mushroom: Mushrooms are Mario's power-up, not Pac-Man's; the only power-up here is the Power Pellet.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Super Star: The invincibility Super Star is from Super Mario Bros.; Pac-Man's only temporary power comes from flashing pellets.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Banana: Bananas arrived in Ms. Pac-Man, whose fruits include pretzels, pears and bananas, but the original stops at melon.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Ring: Rings are Sonic's lifeline in Sega games, not collectible in Namco's maze chase.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Rupee: Rupees are the currency in The Legend of Zelda; Pac-Man never earns money, just dot points.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Coin: Coins are a Mario staple, but Pac-Man eats small dots, not coins; the dots count towards points.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Heart: Hearts are Zelda's health meter, but Pac-Man has no health; he just loses a life when a ghost touches him.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Barrel: Barrels are the enemy in Donkey Kong, the 1981 hit that made Mario's debut as Jumpman; Pac-Man dodges ghosts, not barrels.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Fireball: Fireballs belong to Mario with a Fire Flower; Pac-Man has no way to attack, only avoid or eat blue ghosts.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Flag: The goal flag is Mario's level end; Pac-Man levels end when all 244 items in the maze are eaten.
Things in the original Pac-Man arcade ga.Shell: Shells are Mario Kart ammunition; Pac-Man's maze has no weapons of any kind, only ghosts and dots.

Things that are square or cube-shaped.Chessboard: Chess is played on 64 squares, and the number of possible games is so vast that it exceeds the estimated atoms in the observable universe.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Sticky note: The Post-it came from a glue that failed to stick firmly, developed at 3M in 1968 and turned into a product by a colleague in the 1970s.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Saltine: Saltines have 13 small holes and a square shape, and the holes keep the dough from puffing up into bubbles while baking.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Pizza box: The box is square even though the pizza inside is round, and the corners leave space for tucking in napkins or sauce.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Scrabble tile: Standard English Scrabble has 100 tiles, and the Q is worth ten points, while blank tiles score nothing.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Cheese single: Individually wrapped processed cheese slices were popularized in the 1950s, and their square shape fits neatly on a slice of bread.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Rubik's Cube: Invented by Hungarian Ernő Rubik in 1974, it has over 43 quintillion possible positions, yet it can always be solved in 20 moves or fewer.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Dice: Cube-shaped dice date back about 5,000 years, and standard ones are arranged so opposite faces add up to seven.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Sugar cube: The sugar cube was invented in 1843 by Jakub Kryštof Rad, a Swiss-born manager of a sugar factory in Bohemia, after his wife cut her finger.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Bouillon cube: The stock cube concentrates dried meat or vegetable extract and salt, and the first were sold in Switzerland in the 1900s.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Coin: It's round, not square, a shape that lets vending machines and pockets handle coins easily, though some have 7 sides like the British 50p.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Pizza: Pizza is a classic round pie, with a shape that comes from tossing the dough in the air, although Sicilian-style pies are rectangular.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Egg: An egg is an oval, and its asymmetry means that when nudged it rolls in a tight circle, not a straight line, so it rarely rolls away.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Football: A soccer ball has a sphere made of panels, with the classic design using 32 patches, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Banana: Bananas are long and curved, and grow in clusters called hands, pointing up toward the sun rather than hanging down.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Pencil: Most pencils are hexagonal or round, and the hexagon keeps them from rolling off the desk while being comfortable to hold.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Dinner plate: Circular plates are easy to make on a wheel and clean, and a flat round shape helps heat food evenly.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Tennis ball: A tennis ball is a sphere, and the felt and fuzz slow it through the air, so the shape never makes it a cube.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Yield sign: Another trap: it is a triangle, not a square, unlike the diamond-shaped warning signs that are squares rotated 45 degrees.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Hula hoop: A hoop is a circle, a shape known since ancient times, when children rolled hoops of wood or metal with sticks.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Basketball: A basketball is a sphere about 24 centimeters across with pebbled leather, and the grooves help players grip.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Envelope: An envelope is a rectangle, and its pointed flap is a triangle, which fools many players into thinking it counts as square.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Dollar bill: A US bill is a rectangle about 6.1 by 2.6 inches, and its size hasn't changed since 1929.
Things that are square or cube-shaped.Door: A standard door is a rectangle, usually about 80 inches tall, a size that has barely changed in a century.

Things on an old pirate ship.Cannon: Pirate cannons were often small and swivel-mounted to fire grapeshot at crews; the goal was usually to scare a merchant into surrendering, not sink it.
Things on an old pirate ship.Plank: Walking the plank is mostly a pirate legend from fiction; real pirates more often just threw captives overboard or ransomed them.
Things on an old pirate ship.Crow's nest: The lookout perch high on the mast was named for the crow's nest said to be carried by Viking ships, whose birds were released to find land.
Things on an old pirate ship.Jolly Roger: The skull-and-crossbones flag was meant as a terror tactic; a plain black flag could mean a ship would be spared if it surrendered, while a red one meant no mercy.
Things on an old pirate ship.Anchor: Anchors have held ships since antiquity, and the weight alone isn't enough: flukes dig into the seabed to grip it.
Things on an old pirate ship.Treasure chest: Few real pirates buried treasure; Captain Kidd is one of the few known to have done so, and most loot was spent fast on shore.
Things on an old pirate ship.Cutlass: The short, curved sword was favored for fighting on crowded decks and for cutting rope and cane as much as people.
Things on an old pirate ship.Spyglass: The telescope was invented in the Netherlands around 1608, so classic pirates in the golden age had them but earlier ones didn't.
Things on an old pirate ship.Sails: A pirate sloop could carry vast canvas for speed, and pirates often chose fast, shallow-drafted ships to outrun navy vessels.
Things on an old pirate ship.Rum barrel: Sailors received a daily rum ration, and the Royal Navy kept it until 1970, giving rise to 'Navy rum' brands.
Things on an old pirate ship.Hammock: Sailors adopted hammocks from the Caribbean peoples whom Columbus met, because they swing with the ship's roll.
Things on an old pirate ship.Ship's wheel: Before wheels in the 1700s, ships were steered with a tiller, a long wooden lever pushed by hand.
Things on an old pirate ship.Brig: Besides being a two-masted ship type, 'brig' also means a ship's jail, because brigs were once used to hold prisoners.
Things on an old pirate ship.Outboard motor: Invented around 1907 by Ole Evinrude, who wanted to reach his sweetheart with ice cream on a hot day, so no pirate had one.
Things on an old pirate ship.Sonar: Developed in the early 1900s after the Titanic disaster and in WWI against submarines, so it came centuries too late.
Things on an old pirate ship.Radar: It was developed in the 1930s, so no pirate ship used radio waves to detect other ships.
Things on an old pirate ship.Satellite dish: Space satellites didn't exist until Sputnik in 1957, so they could never be on an old pirate ship.
Things on an old pirate ship.Propeller: The screw propeller was patented in the 1830s, long after the golden age of piracy in the early 1700s.
Things on an old pirate ship.Jet engine: Jet engines weren't flown until the 1930s and 40s, far from the age of sail.
Things on an old pirate ship.GPS: GPS satellites didn't enter service until the 1990s, so old pirates navigated with stars, compasses, and guesswork.
Things on an old pirate ship.Smokestack: Steam ships came in the 1800s, after the age of sail, so a pirate ship ran on wind, with no chimney.
Things on an old pirate ship.Air conditioner: Air conditioning was invented in 1902 and arrived long after pirates, who stayed cool only by the sea breeze.
Things on an old pirate ship.Wi-Fi router: Wi-Fi arrived in the late 1990s, and a pirate's only 'network' was harbor gossip.
Things on an old pirate ship.Periscope: Periscopes are for submarines, which were invented much later than the old pirate ship era.

Types of trousers.Jeans: Jeans came from the 1873 patent by Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis, who added copper rivets to stop workmen's pockets from ripping.
Types of trousers.Chinos: The twill cotton was first used for 19th-century military uniforms, and the name is thought to nod to China, an early source of the cloth.
Types of trousers.Cargo pants: Those big thigh pockets began with the British Army, whose late-1930s battledress trousers added a pocket just for maps.
Types of trousers.Jodhpurs: Snug from knee to ankle and roomy at the hips, they are named for Jodhpur in India, where polo-playing nobles wore them.
Types of trousers.Joggers: Originally athletes' kit, these elastic-cuffed trousers left the gym long ago and now get worn by plenty of people who never jog.
Types of trousers.Capris: Named for the island of Capri, these calf-length pants took off in the 1950s when Audrey Hepburn and other stars wore them.
Types of trousers.Sweatpants: The name is literal: this soft cotton jersey was made to soak up an athlete's sweat, and it became everyday wear much later.
Types of trousers.Khakis: The word comes from Urdu for dust-coloured, after British troops in India dyed their uniforms with mud, tea and coffee to blend in.
Types of trousers.Slacks: The name comes from slack, meaning loose, and the term was used in the 1800s for easy-fitting trousers instead of tight breeches.
Types of trousers.Bell-bottoms: Sailors wore flared trousers so they could roll them up on deck, long before the 1960s and 70s made the shape a fashion icon.
Types of trousers.Palazzo pants: Their ultra-wide, skirt-like legs swirl as you walk, and they became a flowing summer staple in the 1960s and 70s.
Types of trousers.Corduroys: The tale that the word comes from French cord du roi, the king's cord, is a myth, and the real origin is unclear.
Types of trousers.Kilt: A kilt is a pleated tartan wraparound that has no legs at all, which is why it is a skirt even though men wear it.
Types of trousers.Sarong: This single length of cloth is wrapped around the waist and falls to the ankles across South and Southeast Asia, with no legs sewn in.
Types of trousers.Tutu: A tutu is a short skirt of layered stiff netting, and ballet's flat 'pancake' version sticks out like a plate.
Types of trousers.Petticoat: This underskirt adds volume beneath a dress, and in Victorian times a full set of petticoats could weigh a lot.
Types of trousers.Blouse: The word comes from French for a workman's smock, and it is a loose top, so it never covers the legs.
Types of trousers.Poncho: This head-through-a-hole cloak comes from the Andes, and the word is Mapuche, a language of Chile.
Types of trousers.Tunic: Roman soldiers and citizens wore this belted, hip-length top as basic daily clothing, and it does not cover the legs.
Types of trousers.Kaftan: This long, flowing robe comes from Persia and the Ottoman world, where it could be a luxury gift from a sultan.
Types of trousers.Cardigan: It is named for the Earl of Cardigan, who led the Light Brigade into its doomed charge, and it is a knitted top layer.
Types of trousers.Toga: The Roman toga was a wool drape that only citizens could wear, and exiles were not allowed to wear one.
Types of trousers.Sari: This unstitched length of cloth, usually about five to nine meters, is draped around the waist and over a shoulder, never tailored into legs.
Types of trousers.Miniskirt: Mary Quant popularised it in 1960s London and named it after her favourite car, the Mini, and it leaves the legs bare.

Playground equipment.Swing: Swings are a physics pendulum: you pump your legs to change your center of mass and add energy with every swing.
Playground equipment.Slide: Playground slides in the early days were often made from metal, which could burn legs in summer, so most are now plastic.
Playground equipment.Seesaw: A lever with the fulcrum in the middle, it is also known in America as the teeter-totter.
Playground equipment.Monkey bars: Brachiation is the term for swinging arm over arm, and the bars are named after gibbons and monkeys.
Playground equipment.Sandbox: Sandboxes date back to 19th-century Germany, where Berlin set up sand piles for kids in the 1850s.
Playground equipment.Merry-go-round: Pushed by hand, it spins and can take plenty of kids at once, often as in an old-fashioned carousel.
Playground equipment.Climbing frame: The frame is made from metal or wood and often has a net or rope that kids climb up.
Playground equipment.Jungle gym: Sebastian Hinton patented it in 1920 in Chicago, naming it after the jungle for kids to play like monkeys.
Playground equipment.Tire swing: An old tire on a rope became a swing in countless backyards and makes use of recycled rubber.
Playground equipment.Spring rider: These animals on a big spring let toddlers bounce back and forth and remain a staple of small playgrounds.
Playground equipment.Treadmill: The first treadmills of 1818 were prison punishments: inmates walked a huge wheel to grind grain, which makes this a gym, not a playground.
Playground equipment.Rowing machine: Rowing machines copy a boat's stroke and work most major muscles, so this is gym gear rather than playground play.
Playground equipment.Ferris wheel: George Ferris built the first for Chicago's 1893 World's Fair to rival the Eiffel Tower, a fairground ride not a playground.
Playground equipment.Bumper cars: Bumper cars came out of the 1920s, when the Dodgem company patented them; they live in fairgrounds.
Playground equipment.Roller coaster: Coaster descendants of Russian ice slides; the first US one opened at Coney Island in 1884, and none are in playgrounds.
Playground equipment.Haunted house: Haunted houses are fairground attractions designed to scare, the opposite of a play area.
Playground equipment.Log flume: Log flumes are amusement-park rides with a big drop and a splash, too big for a playground.
Playground equipment.Teacups: Teacups come from theme parks, where the Mad Hatter's Tea Party spinning ride opened at Disneyland in 1955.
Playground equipment.Drop tower: A drop tower lifts riders and lets go, a thrill ride that never appears among playground equipment.
Playground equipment.Go-kart: Art Ingels built the first go-kart in 1956 in California from lawnmower parts; they belong on tracks.
Playground equipment.Ski lift: Ski lifts take skiers uphill, and chairlifts were adapted from banana-loading equipment, by the story.
Playground equipment.Bowling alley: Ten-pin bowling began in 19th-century America, and an alley belongs to a bowling center, not a park.
Playground equipment.Escalator: Jesse Reno's 1896 Coney Island moving stairway was the first escalator ride, which is not playground gear.
Playground equipment.Hall of mirrors: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles has 357 mirrors; the funfair version is an attraction, not play gear.

Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Santa Claus: Santa comes from the Dutch Sinterklaas, brought to New York by early Dutch settlers.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Father Christmas: In Britain Father Christmas was once pictured in green robes, and he is a feast-day spirit older than Santa.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Sinterklaas: Sinterklaas arrives each November by steamboat from Spain, and Dutch children leave shoes by the chimney.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Ded Moroz: Ded Moroz means Grandfather Frost; he travels with his granddaughter Snegurochka in Russian tradition.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.La Befana: In Italy, a kindly witch flies on a broom and fills stockings on Epiphany, January 5-6.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Christkind: The name means Christ child; the figure is an angelic child who brings gifts in Germany and Austria.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Père Noël: The French Santa leaves presents in shoes by the fireplace, with a name that means Father Christmas.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Papá Noel: In Spanish-speaking countries, Papa Noel brings gifts, as the name means Father Christmas.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Saint Nicholas: He was a real 4th-century bishop of Myra, in what is now Turkey, famed for secret gifts.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Kris Kringle: The name comes from Christkind, a version of the Christ child that English speakers changed.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Joulupukki: In Finland the name means Yule goat, and he lives in Lapland, in Korvatunturi, tradition says.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Easter Bunny: The Easter Bunny brings eggs in spring, not Christmas gifts.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Tooth Fairy: The Tooth Fairy pays for teeth, but does not bring Christmas gifts.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Sandman: The Sandman brings sleep, rather than gifts, in European folklore.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Cupid: Cupid is the Roman god of love, and is tied to Valentine's Day.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Krampus: Krampus is a horned Alpine figure who punishes naughty children, and is not a gift-bringer.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Grinch: The Grinch tried to steal Christmas rather than give gifts, in Dr. Seuss's 1957 book.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Jack Frost: Jack Frost is a personification of winter cold, not a gift-giver.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Leprechaun: A leprechaun is an Irish fairy who guards a pot of gold and is linked to St. Patrick's Day.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Frosty: Frosty is a snowman from a song, not a gift-bringer.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Mother Goose: Mother Goose is the name on nursery rhymes and is not a gift-bringer.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Bogeyman: The bogeyman is a scary monster used to frighten kids and does not bring gifts.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Pied Piper: The Pied Piper led rats from Hamelin, the legend dates to 1284, and has nothing to do with gifts.
Christmas gift-bringers around the world.Rudolph: Rudolph was created in 1939 for a department store booklet, and he pulls the sleigh rather than brings gifts himself.

Fictional materials.Vibranium: The Marvel metal from Wakanda absorbs vibrations and kinetic energy. Captain America's shield is made of it.
Fictional materials.Adamantium: Marvel's near-unbreakable alloy bonded to Wolverine's skeleton. Its name echoes "adamant," from a Greek word for unconquerable.
Fictional materials.Mithril: Tolkien's silvery metal, light as a feather yet harder than steel. Bilbo gave Frodo a mithril shirt that turned aside a spear.
Fictional materials.Kryptonite: The glowing remains of Superman's homeland, Krypton, drain his powers. It debuted on the Superman radio show, not in the comics.
Fictional materials.Unobtanium: The prize mineral mined on Pandora in Avatar. Engineers used the word as slang for any impossibly hard-to-get material long before the film.
Fictional materials.Beskar: The Mandalorian iron in The Mandalorian that can shrug off blasters and even resist a lightsaber.
Fictional materials.Uru: Enchanted Asgardian metal that Marvel's Thor uses for his hammer. It's a fictional invention, not found on any periodic table.
Fictional materials.Valyrian steel: Game of Thrones steel forged with dragonfire and lost magic. It's among the few things that can destroy White Walkers.
Fictional materials.Flubber: Bouncy green goo invented by a professor in the 1961 Disney film The Absent-Minded Professor. Its name is short for "flying rubber."
Fictional materials.Titanium: Real, and as strong as steel but about 45 percent lighter, which is why it's used in jet engines and surgical implants.
Fictional materials.Tungsten: Real, with the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius, which is why it's used for bulb filaments.
Fictional materials.Palladium: Real, and used in catalytic converters, where it has at times been pricier than gold. Not a comic-book metal.
Fictional materials.Rhodium: Real, and one of the most expensive precious metals. It plates jewelry and cleans car exhaust.
Fictional materials.Osmium: Real, and the densest naturally occurring element. A golf-ball-sized lump would weigh nearly a kilogram.
Fictional materials.Gallium: Real, and it melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a lump of it will liquefy in your hand.
Fictional materials.Molybdenum: Real, and used to toughen steel. Its name comes from the Greek word for lead, which it was long confused with.
Fictional materials.Beryllium: Real, light and very stiff, which is why the James Webb Space Telescope's gold-coated mirrors are built on beryllium.
Fictional materials.Cobalt: Real, and its name comes from German "kobold," the mischievous mine goblins miners blamed for its troublesome ore. It also gives blue glass its color.
Fictional materials.Iridium: Real, and one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust. A thin iridium-rich layer worldwide marks the asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs.
Fictional materials.Tantalum: Real, and found in the capacitors of most phones. It's named after Tantalus of Greek myth.
Fictional materials.Promethium: A trap: it sounds mythic, but promethium is real. It's radioactive, almost nonexistent in nature, and named for Prometheus.
Fictional materials.Vanadium: Real, and named after Vanadis, a Norse goddess. Mixing a little into steel makes it much tougher.
Fictional materials.Ruthenium: Real, and named for Ruthenia, the Latin name for a region of Russia. It's used in electronics and hard-wearing alloys.
Fictional materials.Niobium: Real, and used in the superconducting magnets of MRI machines. It was named after Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus.
